chunks.text: **Pharmacology:** the scientific study of how drugs interact with living systems — from the molecular level to the whole patient.
**Drug (medication):** any chemical substance used to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease, or to alter a physiologic process.
**Pharmacologic effect:** a measurable biological change a drug produces (e.g., lower blood pressure).
**Therapeutic effect:** the intended, beneficial pharmacologic effect for a given condition.
**Adverse drug reaction (ADR):** an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses.
**Toxicity:** harmful effects that occur as the dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
**Chemical name:** describes the exact molecular structure (rarely used in clinical practice).
**Generic name:** the official, non-proprietary name assigned to the active drug — one generic name per drug, regardless of manufacturer.
**Brand (trade) name:** the manufacturer's marketed name; the same generic drug may have several brand names, and brand names change between countries.
**Prodrug:** an inactive precursor converted to the active drug in the body (usually by metabolism).
**Poisons** are drugs with almost exclusively harmful effects — but "the dose makes the poison" (Paracelsus): any substance can harm at the wrong dose.
Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug — ADME.
Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body — receptors & effect.
Pharmacogenomics = how genetic variation shapes individual drug response.
Clinical Pharmacology / Toxicology = applying PK/PD to real patients, and the study of poisoning.
This map covers the whole lecture: PK and PD are the two biggest buckets, and nearly everything else (toxicology, pharmacogenomics, therapeutics) sits on top of them.
Drugs bind receptors by **covalent** bonds (strong, often irreversible), **electrostatic** bonds (most common) or **hydrophobic** bonds (weak).
**Chirality:** over half of drugs are mirror-image pairs (enantiomers); one is usually much more potent, yet most are sold as 50:50 mixtures.
**PA students should learn and prescribe by generic name — it is unambiguous, international, and avoids confusing a patient's multiple brand-name products for different drugs.**
Different brand-name products (Tylenol, many combination cold/flu products) can share the same active generic ingredient.
Prescribing and counseling by generic name avoids hiding duplicate therapy — the reason PAs default to generic names.
If a patient says they take "Tylenol" and separately "acetaminophen," check for accidental double-dosing — this previews the acetaminophen toxicity discussion.
Precise vocabulary (generic names, therapeutic vs. adverse effects) protects patients.
More than half of prescriptions in the USA are for generic drugs.
Weak bonds need a precise fit, so they are **more selective**. Aspirin’s covalent bond to platelet cyclooxygenase lasts until new platelets are made.
Acetaminophen (generic) is sold as Tylenol and under many store brands.

chunks.text: Why prescribe by generic name? One drug has ONE generic name but can hide under SEVERAL brand names — so brand-name products can conceal duplicate therapy and cause double-dosing.
Pharmaco**K**inetics = the body **K**eeps the drug moving (ADME). Pharmaco**D**ynamics = what the **D**rug **D**oes to the body.
ADR = **A**t normal **D**oses, **R**eaction is harmful. Toxicity = **T**oo much (exceeds the therapeutic range).
**Efficacy:** how well a drug works under ideal, controlled trial conditions.
**Effectiveness:** how well a drug works in everyday clinical practice, with real-world adherence and comorbidities.
Drug interactions can also reduce real-world effectiveness below trial efficacy.
**Benefit vs. risk:** the central question regulators and prescribers must weigh for every approval and every prescription.
**Adverse-event reporting:** ongoing, voluntary and mandatory reporting systems (e.g., FDA MedWatch) that catch safety signals after approval.
**Double-blind:** neither subjects nor evaluators know who gets drug or placebo. **Crossover:** each subject gets every treatment in turn.
**IRB:** the committee at each trial site that approves the ethics of the study; participants give informed consent.
Where new drugs come from — Natural products: plants, fungi, microbes, marine organisms.
Synthetic & biotech: designed small molecules; recombinant proteins.
Biologics: monoclonal antibodies, gene- and cell-based therapies.
Drug repurposing: an existing approved drug found to treat a new condition.
From discovery to patient: Discovery → Preclinical testing → Clinical trials → FDA review → Approval → Postmarket surveillance.
Most candidate drugs fail somewhere along this pipeline — approval is the exception, not the rule.
Phase I: safety, tolerability, dose-finding — a small group of healthy volunteers.
Phase II: preliminary efficacy and side-effect profile — a few hundred patients with the target condition.
Phase III: confirm efficacy and monitor adverse effects at scale — hundreds to thousands of patients, often multi-site.
Phase IV: postmarketing surveillance after approval — the general prescribed population.
Every approved drug has passed through a structured development and regulatory pipeline (Phases I–IV).
Phase II has the **highest failure rate** — only about 25% of new drugs move on to Phase III.
Phase III usually enrolls **thousands** of patients (Figure 1–6: 1000–6000), often double-blind and crossover, in settings like the drug's eventual use.
Less than one-third of drugs studied in humans survive clinical trials and reach the market.
To see one case of a toxicity occurring 1 in 10,000, several hundred thousand patients may need exposure — so rare effects usually surface only in Phase IV, which has **no fixed duration**.
Marketing requires a **New Drug Application (NDA)** after Phase III; human testing starts only after an **IND** (Investigational New Drug) application.
Strength of evidence: case reports < cohort and case-control studies < **randomized controlled trials** (the gold standard: randomization balances confounders).
Postmarketing surveillance (Phase IV) is where rare adverse effects are often first detected — trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events.

Case: a new medication improves symptoms in 70% of patients with a chronic, non-life-threatening condition, but postmarketing data show serious hepatotoxicity in about 1%. **Would you prescribe it — and does your answer depend on what else is available?**

**Clinical pearl:** risk-benefit analysis is always comparative — a 1% serious-toxicity rate reads very differently if it is the only effective option versus if three safer alternatives already exist.
Ask "compared to what?" rather than judging the number in isolation.
A patent lasts 20 years; after it expires, generics are approved through an **abbreviated new drug application (ANDA)** that requires bioequivalence data.
Placebo responses can occur in as many as 30–40% of subjects — the reason controlled, blinded trials are needed.
Adverse events that are both **serious and unexpected** must be reported to the FDA within 15 days; clinicians can report through MedWatch.
Dietary supplements are regulated as food under DSHEA (1994), so they get no full FDA drug review.
FDA MedWatch — an adverse-event reporting system.

chunks.text: Phase I population: slides say Phase I: a small group of healthy volunteers. Textbook says Phase I: 20–100 healthy volunteers — but if significant toxicity is expected (cancer, AIDS therapy), volunteer **patients with the disease** are used instead.
Phase II size: slides say Phase II: a few hundred patients with the target condition. Textbook says Phase II: a modest number of patients (100–200) with the target disease.
Why are rare adverse effects found after approval? Trials are too small and too short to catch 1-in-10,000 events — so they show up in Phase IV, in the general prescribed population.
Phases by question: **I** = Is it safe (healthy volunteers)? **II** = Is there an effect? **III** = Is it confirmed at scale? **IV** = Is it still safe in everyone?
Effica**C**y = **C**ontrolled conditions. Effecti**V**eness = real-world **V**ariables (adherence, comorbidities).
**Drug target:** the specific molecule a drug binds to produce its effect.
**Receptor:** a protein target whose activation (or blockade) triggers a cellular response.
**Signal transduction:** the chain of molecular events that converts receptor binding into a cellular effect.
**Pharmacologic response:** the measurable downstream result — contraction, secretion, gene transcription, and so on.
Full agonist — maximal receptor activation.
Partial agonist — submaximal activation, even at full receptor occupancy.
Inverse agonist — reduces baseline (constitutive) receptor activity.
Competitive antagonist — reversibly competes with agonist at the same site; overcome by more agonist.
Noncompetitive antagonist — binds elsewhere or irreversibly reduces the maximal effect.
Irreversible antagonist — permanently inactivates the receptor until new receptor is synthesized.
**Kd:** the drug concentration that fills half the receptors; a low Kd means high affinity.
The pathway: drug → target → signal transduction → response. Every pharmacodynamics topic for the rest of the course maps onto this chain.
Receptor concept: Drug + Receptor → Drug-Receptor Complex → Cellular Response.
This single chain underlies agonism, antagonism, potency, and efficacy — all describe different features of this interaction.
Five major drug target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.
Receptors: G-protein-coupled, ligand-gated ion channel, enzyme-linked, nuclear.
Ion channels: directly gate the flow of ions across a membrane.
Enzymes: drugs can inhibit or, less commonly, activate an enzyme's activity.
Transporters & nucleic acids: carrier proteins; or DNA/RNA for some antimicrobials & gene therapies.
Most drugs target receptors or enzymes — ion channels and transporters matter especially for cardiac and CNS drugs.
An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal; a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.
**Spare receptors:** a maximal response can occur without occupying every receptor (e.g., about 90% of cardiac β receptors can be blocked and maximal inotropic response still preserved).
**Irreversible antagonist** effects last until new receptors are made — duration depends on receptor turnover, not drug elimination (phenoxybenzamine for pheochromocytoma).
A partial agonist's lower maximal effect is **not** due to lower affinity — it can occupy all receptors and still produce less response.
**Allosteric modulators** bind a different site from the agonist (e.g., benzodiazepines enhance GABA's effect).
Agonist-induced **desensitization** (tachyphylaxis) and downregulation reduce response with continued exposure.
Targets beyond receptors: **enzymes** (statins on HMG-CoA reductase), **transporters** (digitalis on Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; antidepressants) and **structural proteins** (colchicine on tubulin).
Five signaling mechanisms carry a drug’s message into the cell: intracellular receptor, receptor tyrosine kinase, cytokine receptor (JAK-STAT), ion channel and G protein (compared in the table).
Albuterol is a selective β2-adrenergic receptor agonist.
Binding activates the β2 receptor → increases intracellular cAMP.
Rising cAMP relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation.
**This is the same receptor-to-response logic you will reuse for every agonist drug this term.**
Albuterol bridges introductory pharmacodynamics into the pulmonary pharmacology seen later in the curriculum.
Competitive antagonism is surmountable in real life: exercise or stress raises catecholamines enough to overcome a fixed propranolol dose.
Propranolol markedly slows the heart rate in pheochromocytoma (high catecholamines) but not the resting rate of a trained marathon runner.
Glucocorticoids will not stop an acute asthma attack within minutes: gene-acting drugs need hours to make new proteins.
Phosphodiesterase inhibitors prolong second messengers: milrinone (cAMP) and sildenafil (cGMP).
Albuterol — selective β2-adrenergic agonist (example of agonism).

chunks.text: Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve **right** (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist **lowers the Emax** instead.

A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism — potency falls, but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax.
Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present.
Study-guide distractor: "has no effect on receptor activity whatsoever" matches none of the agonist/antagonist types.

chunks.text: Why can more agonist overcome a competitive antagonist? Both compete **reversibly for the same site** — flood the site with agonist and it wins, so the curve shifts right but the same Emax is still reached.
Why does albuterol open the airways? β2 activation → ↑ intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle relaxes → bronchodilation.
**C**ompetitive = **C**an be outcompeted (shift right). **N**oncompetitive = **N**o full ceiling (lower Emax).
**Potency:** how much drug is required to produce a given effect — a more potent drug needs a lower dose.
**Efficacy (Emax):** the maximum effect a drug can produce, no matter how high the dose goes.
**EC₅₀:** the drug concentration producing 50% of the maximal effect — the standard measure of potency.
**Therapeutic Index (TI) = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic dose in 50% ÷ effective dose in 50%).**
**Quantal dose-response:** ED₅₀ (effective in 50%), TD₅₀ (toxic in 50%), LD₅₀ (lethal in 50% of animals).
**Therapeutic window:** the range between the minimum therapeutic dose and the minimum toxic dose — more practical than TI for dosing a patient.
The sigmoidal dose-response curve: x-axis = log(dose), y-axis = effect. EC₅₀ is on the x-axis; Emax is the plateau — the ceiling effect.
EC₅₀ is read off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax.
Lower EC₅₀ = more potent. Higher Emax = more efficacious.
Potency and efficacy are independent properties — a drug can differ in one without differing in the other.
A curve farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose (greater potency); curves reaching the same plateau height have identical Emax (efficacy).
A wide TI means a large margin between an effective dose and a toxic dose — generally safer to dose.
A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requires careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring.
The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers is the therapeutic index itself.
Dose-response curves describe potency and efficacy.
Potency clinically matters for dosing — not for choosing the "better" drug.
Efficacy clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless.
With a narrow TI, a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic — which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.
Students should be able to name all four narrow-TI drugs without hesitation and know that each requires therapeutic drug monitoring.
No drug causes only a single specific effect — drugs are **selective**, not specific.
Asthma + hypertension on propranolol: nonselective β blockade can cause bronchoconstriction; a β₁-selective blocker (metoprolol) is an alternative.
**Classic narrow-TI drugs: warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin.**

chunks.text: A drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy — potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."
Same Emax + lower dose needed = MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."
EC₅₀ measures potency — not toxicity and not bioavailability.
A narrow-TI drug is not "safer because it needs a lower dose" — it has a smaller margin and needs closer monitoring.
Definition · Potency: How much drug is needed to get an effect · Efficacy (Emax): The maximum effect the drug can produce
Measured by · Potency: EC₅₀ — **lower EC₅₀ = more potent** · Efficacy (Emax): Plateau height — **higher Emax = more efficacious**
On the curve · Potency: Curve farther **left** · Efficacy (Emax): Curve plateaus **higher**
Clinical weight · Potency: Matters for **dosing**, not for picking the "better" drug · Efficacy (Emax): Matters **much more** — potent + low efficacy may be useless
ED₅₀ vs. TD₅₀ · Wide TI: Far apart — large safety margin · Narrow TI: Close together — small safety margin

chunks.text: Why do narrow-TI drugs need blood levels? The effective dose and the toxic dose sit so close together that a small dosing error can push the patient from effective to toxic.
Why does efficacy beat potency clinically? Potency only changes the dose you give; efficacy sets the ceiling of what the drug can achieve at any dose.
Narrow-TI drugs — "**W**atch **L**evels **D**uring **P**rescribing": **W**arfarin, **L**ithium, **D**igoxin, **P**henytoin.
TI = **T**oxic over **E**ffective → TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀ (toxic on top).
A — Absorption: movement of drug from the site of administration into the bloodstream.
D — Distribution: movement of drug from blood into tissues.
M — Metabolism: chemical transformation of drug, mainly in the liver.
E — Excretion: removal of drug/metabolites from the body, mainly via the kidney.
**Bioavailability (F) = the fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.**
First-pass effect: the liver metabolizes (can inactivate a large fraction of) an orally absorbed drug before it reaches systemic circulation.
**Volume of distribution (Vd):** a calculated value relating total drug in the body to plasma concentration — a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution.
**pKa:** the pH at which a drug is half ionized and half nonionized.
ADME is the organizing skeleton for the rest of the lecture — each remaining pharmacokinetics section is one ADME letter in depth.
ADME determines how much drug reaches its target and for how long.
Metabolism (M arrow → liver) and Excretion (E arrow → kidney) are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug; Absorption and Distribution govern how the drug arrives and spreads.
First-pass route: oral drug → GI tract → portal circulation → liver → systemic circulation.
By definition, an IV dose has 100% bioavailability — the entire dose enters the bloodstream directly (no absorption step).
Oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by first-pass hepatic metabolism.
**Plasma protein binding:** only unbound ("free") drug is pharmacologically active and able to cross membranes.
**Lipid solubility:** lipophilic drugs cross membranes more readily and distribute into fatty tissue.
**Tissue perfusion:** highly perfused organs (brain, heart, kidney) receive drug faster than poorly perfused tissue (fat, bone).
Vd is a theoretical volume, not a real anatomic space.
Blood-brain barrier — **Why can some drugs readily enter the CNS while others cannot?** Tight junctions between endothelial cells restrict paracellular movement.
Small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross the BBB more easily than large, polar, or highly protein-bound drugs.
Efflux transporters (like P-glycoprotein) can actively pump some drugs back out of the CNS.
First-pass loss can happen in the **gut wall** (e.g., intestinal CYP3A4) as well as the liver; grapefruit juice inhibits gut-wall metabolism and P-glycoprotein, raising absorption of some drugs.
**P-glycoprotein (MDR1)** pumps drugs out of cells in brain, testes, and gut; inhibiting it raises digoxin blood levels.
**Ion trapping:** weak acids are excreted faster in **alkaline** urine; weak bases faster in **acidic** urine.
Drugs cross membranes by **lipid diffusion** (the main route), aqueous pores, **carriers** (saturable) or endocytosis (vitamin B₁₂, iron).
Only the **nonionized** form crosses lipid membranes: a weak acid is mostly nonionized when pH < pKa, a weak base when pH > pKa (Henderson-Hasselbalch).
Routes that bypass first-pass metabolism: essentially everything except oral — IV, sublingual, inhaled, transdermal, topical, SC, IM.
Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver's first-pass metabolism; oral dosing passes through the liver first.
Because the liver can inactivate a large fraction of drug first, some drugs are given sublingually or transdermally instead of orally.
A highly polar antibiotic would generally not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis.
Aspirin overdose: sodium bicarbonate alkalinizes blood and urine, reducing aspirin entry into tissues and speeding its renal excretion.
Large first-pass effect: nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine — all require higher oral doses (or a non-oral route) to achieve the same systemic exposure as IV.

chunks.text: Why is IV bioavailability 100%? The whole dose enters the bloodstream directly — there is no absorption step and no trip through the liver first.
Why does sublingual skip first-pass? It drains into systemic veins, not the portal vein — so the drug reaches the body before the liver can inactivate it.
Why do highly protein-bound drugs act less and cross the BBB poorly? Only free (unbound) drug is active and able to cross membranes.
Big first-pass drugs "**N**eed **P**lenty **M**ore by mouth": **N**itroglycerin, **P**ropranolol, **M**orphine.
Drug metabolism = how the body chemically transforms drugs.
Phase I — Functionalization: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis.
Phase II — Conjugation: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione conjugation.
**Enzyme inhibition:** a drug slows a CYP enzyme, raising the blood level of any drug that CYP normally clears.
**Enzyme induction:** a drug increases CYP enzyme production, lowering the blood level (and effect) of drugs that CYP clears.
**Cytochrome P450** (in the liver’s smooth endoplasmic reticulum) does most Phase I work and has low substrate specificity: lipid-soluble drugs are its common thread.
Why metabolize? To inactivate an active drug, making it easier to excrete.
To activate a prodrug into its active form.
To produce an active metabolite that contributes to (or extends) the drug effect.
**Occasionally to produce a toxic metabolite — the basis of some drug-induced organ injury.**
Phase I is primarily carried out by cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes and often creates or unmasks a reactive functional group.
Phase II attaches a polar group to the molecule, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion.
Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always — some drugs go straight to conjugation.
Inhibition slows clearance (substrate level rises); induction speeds clearance (substrate level falls).

Acetaminophen is mostly conjugated (glucuronide/sulfate); in overdose glutathione is depleted and the toxic metabolite (NAPQI) injures the liver — **N-acetylcysteine** given within 8–16 hours protects against fulminant hepatotoxicity.
Share of liver P450: CYP3A4 about 30%, CYP2C9 about 20%, CYP1A2 about 15%, CYP2D6 about 5%.
**Commensal gut microbiota** (gut bacteria) metabolize drugs too: they inactivate digoxin, so antibiotics such as erythromycin can double digoxin levels.
An inducer can speed up its own metabolism (**pharmacokinetic tolerance**): the same dose works less over time.
CYP450 interactions are one of the highest-yield concepts in all of pharmacology — nearly every major drug class has at least one clinically important CYP interaction.
**Example: Drug A inhibits CYP3A4 → Drug B (a CYP3A4 substrate) accumulates → toxicity risk rises.**
Inhibition pushes a substrate's level ABOVE 100% of baseline (toxicity risk); induction pushes it BELOW 100% (therapeutic-failure risk).
Inhibiting the CYP that clears a substrate is especially dangerous when the substrate has a narrow therapeutic index.
Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.
Liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis) slows metabolism enough that ordinary doses can cause coma. CYP3A4 handles over 50% of liver-metabolized prescriptions.
**Diet and environment:** smoking, charcoal-broiled food and cruciferous vegetables induce CYP1A; grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A.
Stopping an inducer is as risky as starting one: when the inducer stops, warfarin metabolism slows, levels rise and bleeding can follow.
NAPQI (from acetaminophen) is the textbook example of a toxic metabolite produced by normal Phase I metabolism — previewing the acetaminophen toxicity lecture.

**Glomerular filtration:** free (unbound) drug passes from blood into the renal tubule based on molecular size.
**Tubular secretion:** active transporters move additional drug from blood into the tubule.
**Tubular reabsorption:** lipophilic, un-ionized drug can passively diffuse back into the blood, reducing net elimination.

chunks.text: Why does alkalinizing urine help in aspirin overdose? It keeps the drug ionized in the tubule, and only un-ionized drug can diffuse back — so reabsorption is blocked and more drug leaves.
Why adjust doses in CKD? Less renal function → less clearance → more exposure and accumulation of renally-cleared drugs.
Kidney handling = "**F**ilter, **S**ecrete, **R**eabsorb" — **F**ree drug filtered, **S**ecreted by transporters, **R**eabsorbed if lipophilic & un-ionized.
**Half-life (t½) = the time required for the plasma drug concentration to fall by 50%.**
**Steady state:** the point at which drug intake equals drug elimination; reached in about 4–5 half-lives with regular dosing.
**Loading dose:** a larger initial dose used to rapidly reach a therapeutic concentration, without waiting for steady state.
**Maintenance dose:** the regular, ongoing dose that keeps the drug within the therapeutic range once steady state is reached.
**Clearance = the volume of plasma from which drug is completely removed per unit time.**
**t½ = 0.7 × Vd / CL** — half-life rises when Vd rises or clearance falls.
**Loading dose = Vd × target concentration** (e.g., theophylline: 35 L × 10 mg/L = 350 mg for a 70-kg adult).
**Extraction ratio:** the share of drug the liver removes in one pass. High-ER drugs have low oral bioavailability (morphine ER 0.67 → about 33%).
**Target concentration approach** (the rational way to design a dosage regimen): pick the level that gives the desired effect, then dose from the patient’s clearance and Vd.
**Zero-order absorption** runs at a constant rate (controlled-release forms); **first-order** is proportional to the amount left.
PK calculations = the math PAs actually use at the bedside.
Half-life is determined by clearance and volume of distribution together — it is not a fixed drug "property" independent of physiology.
A drug is roughly 97% eliminated after about 5 half-lives.
**Formula: % remaining = 100% x (1/2)^(number of half-life)** — i.e., per number of half-lives elapsed.
**Formula: C(t) = C₀ x (1/2)^(t/t½)** — C₀ = starting concentration, t = time elapsed.
Worked example (both formulas): t½ = 6 h; an IV dose gives a starting plasma concentration of 100 mg/L — see the table for each half-life.
Clearance determines how efficiently a drug is removed — and, along with Vd, determines half-life.
Total clearance is usually the sum of hepatic and renal clearance.
Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance.
Steady state takes ~4–5 half-lives regardless of dose size — the same reason a drug is ~97% eliminated ~5 half-lives after stopping it.
Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life.
During regular dosing: 50% of steady state after 1 half-life, 75% after 2, and over 90% after 4 — the textbook's "four half-lives" rule of thumb.
**Capacity-limited (saturable) elimination:** clearance falls as concentration rises — important for phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin.
**Maintenance dosing rate = clearance × target concentration** (÷ F if oral). The dosing interval changes only peaks and troughs, not the average level.
Half-life can change without clearance changing: diazepam’s half-life lengthens with age because its Vd grows.
Effects can outlast plasma levels (delayed effects): warfarin acts only as clotting factors turn over.

**Clinical pearl:** reduced clearance raises drug concentration and prolongs half-life; many renally-cleared drugs are managed by extending the dosing interval, reducing the dose, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl.
The logic chain: clearance ↓ → half-life ↑ → time to steady state ↑ → accumulation risk ↑ if the regimen is not adjusted.
Reduced renal clearance raises both drug concentration and half-life.
A loading dose reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives; it does not change the maintenance dose or remove the need for monitoring.
High-extraction drugs (morphine, propranolol, verapamil) vary widely between patients, and far more drug gets through in cirrhosis.
**Schedule matters:** gentamicin is more nephrotoxic as a constant infusion than as intermittent doses at the same average level.
Give IV loading doses slowly (over an hour): a fast bolus can overshoot into toxicity, e.g., phenytoin.
Timing drug levels: digoxin at least 6 hours after the dose; lithium just before the next dose.
In obesity, dose drugs that stay out of fat (gentamicin, digoxin) on fat-free mass.
Displacing a drug from plasma proteins raises free drug only briefly; the body eliminates the extra, so binding changes rarely matter clinically.

**Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation changes an individual's response to a drug.**
Why the same dose does not work the same way in everyone.
**PM, IM, EM, UM:** poor, intermediate, extensive (normal) and ultrarapid metabolizer.
Genetic variation can alter drug metabolism (e.g., CYP enzyme activity).
It can alter drug transport across membranes.
It can alter drug target structure or expression.
It can alter overall drug response and risk of adverse reactions.
Personalized pharmacotherapy combines genotype, phenotype, disease state, and other medications into individualized therapy.
**Pharmacogenomics is one input among several — genotype alone never dictates therapy in isolation.**
Codeine is converted to morphine (200× more potent) by CYP2D6; CPIC recommends an alternative analgesic for CYP2D6 poor **and** ultrarapid metabolizers.
Clopidogrel: about 85% of a dose is inactivated by esterases; CYP2C19 activates the rest. CYP2C19 poor/intermediate metabolizers → prasugrel or ticagrelor.
TPMT intermediate activity: start thiopurines at 30–70% of the target dose; deficient: use a drastically reduced dose or an alternative.
Warfarin dose varies up to 20-fold between patients; CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotypes explain much of it.
**G6PD deficiency** (X-linked): red cells cannot make enough NADPH, so they hemolyze under oxidative stress (infection, fava beans, certain drugs).
NUDT15 variants, like TPMT, cause thiopurine intolerance.
CYP2D6 variation alters metabolism of many antidepressants and opioids (e.g., codeine activation).
CYP2C19 variation affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing.
TPMT deficiency raises toxicity risk with thiopurine drugs (e.g., azathioprine).
Certain HLA alleles sharply raise the risk of severe hypersensitivity to specific drugs.
HLA-B*5801 is associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol — a textbook pharmacogenomic screening consideration (seen again in the gout lecture).

**Inflammatory pain:** pain driven by inflammatory mediators.

**Acute pain:** recent onset, often tied to an identifiable injury or flare.

**COX-1, the “housekeeping” enzyme:** maintains gastric mucosal protection and normal renal blood flow; inhibiting it causes GI and renal adverse effects.

Simplified teaching model, not an absolute separation: COX-1 and COX-2 functions overlap, and COX-2 is also constitutively expressed in the kidney and elsewhere.
**Pathway:** COX converts arachidonic acid to prostaglandins **and thromboxane A2 (TXA2)**. Less prostaglandin: pain, fever, and inflammation fall. Less TXA2: bleeding risk.
Every NSAID shares the COX mechanism; the side effects follow from losing protective prostaglandins (GI injury, platelet inhibition, renal effects).
**COX-1 is constitutive:** gastric mucosa (protection), platelets (TXA2, clotting), kidney (renal blood flow). **COX-2 is inducible** in inflamed tissue: pain, swelling, fever.
Nonselective NSAIDs block both isoforms, so GI injury is common. Selectivity trades anti-inflammatory benefit against GI and platelet protection.
Celecoxib selectively inhibits inducible COX-2, the main source of inflammatory prostaglandins, and largely spares COX-1 in gastric mucosa — lowering ulcer and bleeding risk.
**Celecoxib’s trade-off:** PGI2 (prostacyclin) falls without a matching drop in TXA2, which raises cardiovascular event risk; stomach and platelet protection continue.
Celecoxib still affects kidney prostaglandins, so renal risk is not eliminated.
Aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet COX (the effect lasts the 8–10-day life of the platelet); other nonselective NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.
COX-2 inhibitors spare platelet thromboxane (made by COX-1) but block endothelial prostacyclin — so they are not cardioprotective.

**Osteoarthritis (OA):** primarily degenerative joint disease — cartilage breakdown with mechanical wear.
**Rheumatoid arthritis (RA):** autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease — immune-mediated joint destruction.
**OA pathophysiology:** mechanical load and wear degrade cartilage; bone remodels with osteophytes.
**RA pathophysiology:** immune activation → autoimmune synovitis forms a **pannus** that erodes cartilage and bone; **TNF-α and IL-6** drive the inflammation and joint damage.
OA treatment goal: pain control and function.
RA treatment goal: suppress disease activity, not just pain.
The hinge: OA is managed mainly with analgesics/NSAIDs, while RA requires disease-modifying therapy.
**DMARD (Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drug):** a drug intended to alter the course of RA, not just mask its symptoms.
**Goal of therapy:** slow or halt joint destruction and systemic inflammation, rather than providing analgesia alone.
An NSAID can make a patient feel better without changing the disease trajectory; a DMARD is meant to change the trajectory itself.
**NSAIDs** relieve pain and swelling within days but do not alter joint damage; **DMARDs** take weeks to months to act, then slow cartilage and bone destruction.
**Timing:** judge a DMARD over months, not after the first visit — set expectations that benefit builds over months. Relief now with NSAIDs, protection later with DMARDs.
Targeted therapy: each biologic class corresponds to a different cytokine or cell type in the inflammatory cascade — the mediator list from the start of the lecture.
DMARD effects take 2 weeks to 6 months to appear. Types: conventional synthetic (cs), biologic (b), and targeted synthetic (ts, e.g., tofacitinib).
Biologics are large molecules, usually proteins made by recombinant DNA technology; JAK inhibitors are oral small-molecule targeted synthetic DMARDs.

B-cell targeted therapy depletes or modulates B lymphocytes.
T-cell costimulation modulators block the second signal needed for T-cell activation.
Figure 3: abatacept acts at T-cell activation, TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab at cytokine release, rituximab at B cells — all upstream of synovial inflammation and joint destruction.
**TNF inhibitors:** antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab) and etanercept, a receptor fusion protein, neutralize soluble and membrane TNF-α, preventing TNFR activation.
**Tocilizumab** blocks both membrane and soluble IL-6 receptors.
**Abatacept (CTLA-4-Ig)** binds CD80/86 and blocks CD28 costimulation, acting early at T-cell activation.
**Rituximab (anti-CD20)** binds CD20 and depletes B cells for months.
Each biologic intercepts a different step of the immune cascade: walk it from T-cell activation to cytokines to synovial damage — abatacept acts earliest.
**OA step 1:** acetaminophen — reasonable first-line for mild OA pain.
**OA step 2:** oral NSAIDs (effective, systemic risks) or topical NSAIDs (local relief, much lower systemic exposure).
**Intra-articular corticosteroid injections:** short-term relief for flares in a single joint.
Other approaches: activity modification, physical therapy, weight management.
**Where each OA analgesic acts:** acetaminophen centrally (brain and spinal cord COX) — little anti-inflammatory effect in the joint.
Oral or topical NSAIDs block COX in joint tissue (synovium and cartilage), lowering prostaglandins, pain, and swelling.
An intra-articular steroid calms local inflammation inside the joint for fast, short-term flare relief. Choice depends on which tissue drives the pain.
Methotrexate anchors most RA regimens; leflunomide is the alternative when it is not tolerated.
Rheumatoid arthritis: they modify the disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
TNF inhibitors are the first-line biologic; tocilizumab works as monotherapy; rituximab is used after TNF-inhibitor failure.
**Glucocorticoid drugs in rheumatic diseases:** used chronically in 30–70% of RA patients; relief is prompt and dramatic, and they slow new bone erosions.
Long-term prednisone in RA: no more than 7.5 mg daily, tapered when possible — even 2.8 mg daily for over 5 years is linked to severe infections.
Intra-articular corticosteroids often relieve painful symptoms for up to several months.
Long-term glucocorticoid harms: osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, Cushing syndrome, infections, cataract, glaucoma, gastric ulcer, depression.
Methotrexate starts at 7.5 mg weekly and rises to 15–25 mg weekly; it slows new erosions in RA.
**Combination therapy with DMARDs** is now the rule when monotherapy falls short; triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine) rivals etanercept plus methotrexate.
**Boxed warning — all TNF inhibitors:** possible malignancy, especially lymphoma.

options.D: Phase IV

quiz.why: Phase III trials enroll hundreds to thousands of patients, often at multiple sites, to confirm efficacy and monitor safety at scale before approval. Phase I is small-scale safety/dosing, Phase II is preliminary efficacy, and Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval.
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S16-17

quiz.stem: In Figure 1 above, the dashed curve (+ Competitive antagonist) is shifted to the right of the agonist-alone curve but reaches the same plateau at the top. What does this pattern show?

options.A: More agonist is needed to reach the same effect, but the same maximal effect is still achievable
options.B: The competitive antagonist lowers the drug’s efficacy (Emax)
options.C: The competitive antagonist increases the drug’s potency
options.D: The competitive antagonist has no measurable effect on the agonist’s curve

quiz.why: A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism: it takes more drug to reach a given effect (potency falls), but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax. Contrast this with the noncompetitive/irreversible curve in the same figure, which plateaus lower instead of shifting right.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S24-25

quiz.stem: A drug binds the same receptor as an endogenous agonist and lowers the tissue’s baseline (constitutive) activity below normal, without any agonist present. This drug is best classified as a(n):

options.A: Full agonist
options.B: Partial agonist
options.C: Competitive antagonist
options.D: Inverse agonist

quiz.why: An inverse agonist actively reduces constitutive (baseline) receptor activity below normal — a true antagonist merely blocks the agonist without lowering baseline activity itself.
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S27-28

quiz.stem: On the dose-response curve in Figure 2, the point marked EC₅₀ sits exactly halfway up the rising part of the curve. What does this point represent?

options.A: The dose at which the drug becomes toxic
options.B: The concentration producing 50% of the drug’s maximal effect
options.C: The point where the drug has zero effect
options.D: The drug’s bioavailability

quiz.why: EC₅₀ is read directly off the curve at the halfway point between baseline and Emax (the plateau) — it is the standard graphical measure of potency, not a measure of toxicity or bioavailability.
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S32-33

quiz.stem: In the left panel of Figure 3, Drug A’s curve sits to the left of Drug B’s curve, but both curves plateau at the same height. What does this tell you?

options.A: Drug A is more potent than Drug B, and both have equal efficacy
options.B: Drug A is more efficacious than Drug B
options.C: Drug A and Drug B have different Emax values
options.D: Drug B is more potent than Drug A

quiz.why: A curve positioned farther left reaches the same effect at a lower dose — that is greater potency. Because both curves reach the same plateau height, their Emax (efficacy) is identical; only potency differs, exactly as the right panel then shows the reverse case (same potency, different efficacy).
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S36-37

quiz.stem: Comparing the two number lines in Figure 4, the narrow-TI drug’s ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers sit much closer together than the wide-TI drug’s. What is the clinical implication?

options.A: The narrow-TI drug is safer because it requires a lower dose
options.B: The narrow-TI drug has a smaller margin between an effective and a toxic dose, requiring closer monitoring
options.C: The wide-TI drug is more likely to cause toxicity
options.D: Therapeutic index has no bearing on dosing safety

quiz.why: The distance between the ED₅₀ and TD₅₀ markers on the number line is the therapeutic index itself — a narrow gap (as with warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin) means a small dosing error can move a patient from effective to toxic, which is why these drugs require blood-level monitoring.
quiz.label: Lecture check 7 · S40-41

quiz.stem: Drug X requires a much lower dose than Drug Y to achieve the same effect, but both drugs achieve the same maximum effect (Emax). Which statement is correct?

options.A: Drug X is more efficacious than Drug Y
options.B: Drug X is more potent than Drug Y
options.C: Drug X has a narrower therapeutic index than Drug Y
options.D: Drug X and Drug Y have different Emax values

quiz.why: Needing a lower dose for the same effect is the definition of greater potency. Since both drugs reach the same Emax, their efficacy is equal — potency and efficacy are independent properties.
quiz.label: Lecture check 8 · S42-43

quiz.stem: In Figure 5, two separate arrows leave the Central Compartment box: one labeled "M" pointing to Metabolism (Liver), and one labeled "E" pointing to Excretion (Kidney). Together, these two arrows represent which part of ADME?

options.A: Absorption and Distribution
options.B: Distribution only
options.C: Metabolism and Excretion — how the drug is transformed and cleared
options.D: Only the Excretion step

quiz.why: The diagram shows drug leaving the Central Compartment by two separate routes: the "M" arrow to the liver (biotransformation) and the "E" arrow to the kidney (elimination). Together these are the back half of ADME — how the body gets rid of the drug, as opposed to Absorption and Distribution, which govern how the drug arrives and spreads.
quiz.label: Lecture check 9 · S47-48

quiz.stem: Which route of administration bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism entirely, by entering systemic venous circulation directly?

options.A: Sublingual
options.B: Oral, taken on an empty stomach
options.C: All routes undergo first-pass metabolism equally
options.D: Oral, taken with food

quiz.why: Sublingual absorption enters systemic venous circulation directly, bypassing the portal vein and the liver’s first-pass metabolism — unlike oral dosing, which is absorbed into the portal circulation and passes through the liver first.
quiz.label: Lecture check 10 · S54-55

quiz.stem: A 45-year-old patient takes a new medication exactly as prescribed. Drug levels are within the therapeutic range, yet the patient develops an unintended, harmful response. Which term best describes this event?

options.A: Toxicity, because any harmful drug response counts as toxicity
options.B: An adverse drug reaction, because it occurred at a normal therapeutic dose
options.C: A therapeutic effect, because the drug was taken exactly as prescribed
options.D: A pharmacologic effect only, because it was a measurable biological change
options.E: Irreversible antagonism, because the receptor was permanently inactivated

quiz.why: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses (S5).

whys.A: Toxicity is harm that occurs as dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range (S5); here levels were within range.
whys.B: An ADR is an unintended and harmful response occurring at normal therapeutic doses (S5).
whys.C: A therapeutic effect is the intended, beneficial effect (S5); this response was unintended and harmful.
whys.D: Every ADR is a pharmacologic effect, but 'unintended and harmful at normal doses' is the more specific, best answer (S5).
whys.E: Irreversible antagonism describes receptor inactivation until new receptor is synthesized (S22) — not a type of adverse event.

quiz.label: Q1 · Clinical vignette · The Language of Pharmacology

quiz.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes pharmacokinetics from pharmacodynamics?

options.A: Pharmacokinetics studies receptor binding; pharmacodynamics studies absorption and excretion
options.B: Pharmacokinetics applies only to IV drugs; pharmacodynamics applies only to oral drugs
options.C: Pharmacokinetics studies genetic variation; pharmacodynamics studies poisoning and overdose
options.D: Pharmacokinetics is what the drug does to the body; pharmacodynamics is what the body does to the drug
options.E: Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body

quiz.why: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect) (S6).

whys.A: Receptors & effect belong to PD; absorption and excretion (ADME) belong to PK (S6).
whys.B: Neither branch is defined by route; PK covers ADME for any route (S6, S49).
whys.C: Genetic variation = pharmacogenomics; poisoning = clinical pharmacology/toxicology (S6).
whys.D: This reverses the definitions (S6).
whys.E: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect) (S6).

quiz.label: Q2 · Mechanism · The Language of Pharmacology

quiz.stem: A drug relieved symptoms in most participants of a controlled multi-site trial. In your clinic, far fewer patients improve; many miss doses and have several comorbidities. Which concept best explains the gap?

options.A: A narrow therapeutic index that appeared after approval
options.B: Lower potency than was measured during trial dose-finding
options.C: Extensive first-pass metabolism in the clinic's patients
options.D: Competitive antagonism of the drug by the comorbid conditions
options.E: Real-world effectiveness falling below the drug's trial efficacy

quiz.why: Efficacy is performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness is performance in everyday practice with real-world adherence and comorbidities (S14).

whys.A: TI describes the gap between effective and toxic doses (S38), not missed doses or comorbidities.
whys.B: Potency is the dose needed for an effect and matters for dosing, not for whether patients improve (S34).
whys.C: First-pass effect lowers oral bioavailability (S50-51); it doesn't explain adherence- and comorbidity-driven differences.
whys.D: Competitive antagonism is a drug competing at the same receptor site (S22), not a disease effect.
whys.E: Efficacy is performance under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness is performance in everyday practice with real-world adherence and comorbidities (S14).

quiz.label: Q3 · Clinical vignette · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: Two years after approval, reports reveal a serious reaction occurring in about 1 in 10,000 patients — never seen in the clinical trials. Which best explains why it was missed before approval?

options.A: Adverse-event reporting systems accept only voluntary reports
options.B: Approval came before the drug completed any clinical trial phase
options.C: Phase I trials enrolled patients who already had the target condition
options.D: Trial populations were too small and too short to detect so rare an event
options.E: Phase III trials are not designed to monitor adverse effects

quiz.why: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events (S12 notes).

whys.A: Reporting systems are both voluntary and mandatory (S14).
whys.B: Approved drugs pass through a structured pipeline with clinical trials before FDA review (S12, S56).
whys.C: Phase I uses a small group of healthy volunteers (S13).
whys.D: Rare adverse effects are often first detected in Phase IV because trial populations are too small and too short in duration to catch 1-in-10,000 events (S12 notes).
whys.E: Phase III confirms efficacy AND monitors adverse effects at scale (S13).

quiz.label: Q4 · Clinical vignette · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: According to the textbook, which clinical trial phase has the highest rate of drug failures?

options.A: Phase II
options.B: Phase IV
options.C: FDA review
options.D: Phase III
options.E: Phase I

quiz.why: Phase II has the highest failure rate; only about 25% of drugs move on to Phase III (p. 17).

whys.A: Phase II has the highest failure rate; only about 25% of drugs move on to Phase III (p. 17).
whys.B: Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval (p. 17).
whys.C: FDA review is the approval step after Phase III, not a trial phase (p. 17).
whys.D: Phase III confirms efficacy in thousands, after most failures have occurred (p. 17).
whys.E: Phase I sets the safe dose range in 20–100 subjects; it is not the main failure point (p. 17).

quiz.label: Q5 · Mechanism · Drug Development & Regulation

quiz.stem: A 22-year-old patient inhales albuterol, and within minutes the bronchial smooth muscle relaxes. Which sequence best explains this effect?

options.A: β2 receptor blockade → falling intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.B: Enzyme inhibition → falling intracellular cAMP → bronchial smooth muscle dilation
options.C: β2 receptor activation → rising intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation
options.D: Ion channel opening → rising intracellular cAMP → smooth muscle contraction
options.E: Inverse agonism at β2 → lowered baseline activity → smooth muscle relaxation

quiz.why: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: binding activates β2 → increases cAMP → relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation (S26).

whys.A: Albuterol is an agonist — it activates, not blocks, β2, and cAMP rises (S26).
whys.B: The mechanism is receptor activation with rising cAMP (S26).
whys.C: Albuterol is a selective β2 agonist: binding activates β2 → increases cAMP → relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation (S26).
whys.D: Albuterol acts on the β2 receptor, and the result is relaxation, not contraction (S26).
whys.E: Inverse agonists reduce baseline activity (S22); albuterol is a selective β2 agonist (S26).

quiz.label: Q6 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A patient receives a drug that blocks a receptor. Raising the dose of the agonist medication eventually restores the full original maximal response. The blocking drug is most likely a(n):

options.A: Noncompetitive antagonist
options.B: Inverse agonist
options.C: Irreversible antagonist
options.D: Competitive antagonist
options.E: Partial agonist

quiz.why: A competitive antagonist reversibly competes at the same site and is overcome by more agonist — same Emax, curve shifted right (S22, S22 notes).

whys.A: Noncompetitive antagonists reduce the maximal effect, so full Emax is not restored (S22).
whys.B: An inverse agonist lowers baseline activity; the scenario describes surmountable blockade (S22, S28).
whys.C: Irreversible antagonists permanently inactivate receptors until new ones are synthesized, lowering Emax (S22, S22 notes).
whys.D: A competitive antagonist reversibly competes at the same site and is overcome by more agonist — same Emax, curve shifted right (S22, S22 notes).
whys.E: A partial agonist itself gives submaximal activation (S22); it is not described as a blocker overcome by more agonist.

quiz.label: Q7 · Mechanism · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A 54-year-old is given phenoxybenzamine before surgery for pheochromocytoma. Blood pressure stays controlled even when the tumor releases large catecholamine surges. What best explains why the blockade persists?

options.A: It activates opposing receptors, producing a physiologic counter-effect instead
options.B: It binds receptors irreversibly; effect lasts until new receptors are made
options.C: It is a partial agonist that caps the maximal catecholamine response
options.D: It neutralizes catecholamines chemically in plasma before they reach receptors
options.E: It competes reversibly, so high catecholamine levels easily displace it

quiz.why: An irreversible antagonist's duration depends on receptor turnover, and high agonist levels cannot overcome it (p. 25).

whys.A: That is physiologic antagonism, like insulin vs glucocorticoids (p. 27).
whys.B: An irreversible antagonist's duration depends on receptor turnover, and high agonist levels cannot overcome it (p. 25).
whys.C: Partial agonists produce a submaximal response; phenoxybenzamine is an irreversible antagonist (p. 25; p. 26).
whys.D: That is chemical antagonism, like protamine–heparin (p. 26).
whys.E: That describes competitive antagonism, which surges CAN overcome (p. 25).

quiz.label: Q8 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A patient asks why an inhaled bronchodilator works in minutes but an oral corticosteroid takes hours. What best explains the corticosteroid’s delay?

options.A: It acts on an intracellular receptor that changes gene transcription
options.B: It is a partial agonist with low efficacy
options.C: It acts on a ligand-gated ion channel
options.D: It must first be activated by CYP2D6
options.E: It binds a G protein–coupled receptor that raises cAMP

quiz.why: Gene-acting drugs need time to make new proteins, so effects lag 30 minutes to several hours (p. 28).

whys.A: Gene-acting drugs need time to make new proteins, so effects lag 30 minutes to several hours (p. 28).
whys.B: Efficacy does not explain timing (p. 28).
whys.C: Ion channels respond within milliseconds (p. 31).
whys.D: Prodrug activation is not the reason for this lag (p. 28).
whys.E: That is how a β₂ agonist bronchodilator works, quickly (p. 31; p. 32).

quiz.label: Q9 · Mechanism · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A drug activates a receptor coupled to Gq. Which change follows inside the cell?

options.A: Adenylyl cyclase is stimulated, so cAMP rises
options.B: Phospholipase C makes IP₃ and DAG; calcium rises
options.C: Phosphodiesterase breaks down cGMP in the cell
options.D: A JAK kinase activates STAT transcription proteins
options.E: Adenylyl cyclase is inhibited, so cAMP falls

quiz.why: Gq stimulates phospholipase C, producing IP₃ (calcium release) and DAG (protein kinase C) (p. 32; p. 35).

whys.A: That is Gs (p. 32).
whys.B: Gq stimulates phospholipase C, producing IP₃ (calcium release) and DAG (protein kinase C) (p. 32; p. 35).
whys.C: That is Gt in the retina (p. 32).
whys.D: That is a cytokine receptor, not a G protein (p. 29).
whys.E: That is Gi (p. 32).

quiz.label: Q10 · Mechanism · Pharmacodynamics: Targets & Receptors

quiz.stem: A PA is starting a patient on lithium. Compared with a drug that has a wide therapeutic index, what does lithium's narrow therapeutic index mean for this patient's care?

options.A: Lithium is more potent, so it can be dosed without monitoring levels
options.B: Lithium has a higher Emax, so lower doses than usual are always enough
options.C: Lithium is 100% bioavailable, so blood levels never need to be checked
options.D: Effective and toxic doses are close, so dose carefully and monitor blood levels
options.E: Lithium has a large safety margin, so dosing errors are well tolerated

quiz.why: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requiring careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring; lithium is a classic narrow-TI drug (S38).

whys.A: Potency matters for dosing amount, not safety margin; narrow-TI drugs need monitoring (S34, S38).
whys.B: TI is about toxic vs. effective doses, not Emax (S30, S38).
whys.C: Bioavailability is a different concept (S50); narrow-TI drugs need monitoring (S38).
whys.D: A narrow TI means effective and toxic doses are close together — requiring careful dosing and often blood-level monitoring; lithium is a classic narrow-TI drug (S38).
whys.E: That describes a WIDE TI (S38).

quiz.label: Q11 · Clinical vignette · Dose-Response Relationships

quiz.stem: Two drugs relieve the same symptom. Drug A works at 5 mg and Drug B at 50 mg, but at maximal doses Drug B produces a much greater maximal effect. Which statement best guides drug selection?

options.A: Drug B has greater efficacy, which matters more clinically than Drug A's potency
options.B: Drug A should be chosen because greater potency means it works better
options.C: Both drugs have equal efficacy because both relieve the same symptom
options.D: Drug A has greater efficacy because it needs a much smaller dose
options.E: Drug B has greater potency because its maximal effect is much higher

quiz.why: Efficacy (Emax) clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless (S34).

whys.A: Efficacy (Emax) clinically matters much more than potency — a highly potent drug with low efficacy may be clinically useless (S34).
whys.B: Potency alone never tells you whether a drug works better (S34 notes).
whys.C: Drug B reaches a higher maximal effect, so its efficacy is greater (S30).
whys.D: A smaller dose means greater POTENCY; efficacy is the maximum effect (S30).
whys.E: Higher Emax = more efficacious, not more potent (S34).

quiz.label: Q12 · Clinical vignette · Dose-Response Relationships

quiz.stem: A patient stable on IV propranolol is switched to the oral form and needs a much higher oral dose to reach the same systemic exposure. Which best explains this?

options.A: Propranolol has a narrow therapeutic index, so oral doses must be higher
options.B: Extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism lowers the drug's oral bioavailability
options.C: Propranolol is highly protein-bound, so the oral form is inactive in plasma
options.D: The IV form was less than 100% bioavailable, so less drug reached the blood
options.E: Oral propranolol cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so more must be given

quiz.why: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect; oral doses pass GI → portal → liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV exposure (S51, S50).

whys.A: Narrow TI calls for careful dosing and monitoring (S38); propranolol is named for first-pass, not narrow TI (S51).
whys.B: Propranolol has a large first-pass effect; oral doses pass GI → portal → liver before systemic circulation, so higher oral doses are needed to match IV exposure (S51, S50).
whys.C: Protein binding affects free drug in plasma regardless of route (S52); the IV-to-oral gap is the first-pass effect (S51).
whys.D: IV has 100% bioavailability by definition (S50).
whys.E: BBB crossing relates to CNS entry (S53), not systemic exposure after an oral dose.

quiz.label: Q13 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution

quiz.stem: A patient with meningitis receives a highly polar antibiotic. Which statement best describes this drug's ability to reach the CNS?

options.A: Polar drugs never reach the CNS, even when the meninges are inflamed
options.B: Polar drugs cross easily because P-glycoprotein pumps them into the CNS
options.C: Polar drugs usually cross poorly, but inflamed meninges allow better entry
options.D: Polar drugs cross easily because tight junctions favor polar molecules
options.E: Polar drugs cross well because the brain is a poorly perfused tissue

quiz.why: A highly polar antibiotic generally would not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis (S53 notes).

whys.A: Inflamed meninges (meningitis) are the stated exception (S53 notes).
whys.B: Efflux transporters like P-glycoprotein pump some drugs back OUT of the CNS (S53).
whys.C: A highly polar antibiotic generally would not cross the BBB well — unless the meninges are inflamed, as in meningitis (S53 notes).
whys.D: Tight junctions restrict paracellular movement; small lipophilic non-ionized drugs cross more easily (S53).
whys.E: The brain is highly perfused (S52), and perfusion does not overcome the BBB for polar drugs (S53).

quiz.label: Q14 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution

quiz.stem: A patient overdoses on a weak-acid drug. To speed its renal excretion, what should be done to the urine?

options.A: Make the urine more acidic
options.B: Slow glomerular filtration
options.C: Keep urine pH unchanged and give more fluids only
options.D: Raise plasma protein binding
options.E: Make the urine more alkaline

quiz.why: In alkaline urine a weak acid is mostly ionized, so it cannot diffuse back across the tubule and is trapped in the urine (p. 10).

whys.A: Acidic urine keeps a weak acid nonionized and lipid-soluble, so more is reabsorbed (p. 10).
whys.B: Less filtration would slow excretion, not speed it (p. 10).
whys.C: Fluids alone do not trap the drug; ionization is the lever (p. 10).
whys.D: Protein binding does not trap drug in the urine (p. 8; p. 10).
whys.E: In alkaline urine a weak acid is mostly ionized, so it cannot diffuse back across the tubule and is trapped in the urine (p. 10).

quiz.label: Q15 · Clinical vignette · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution

quiz.stem: In Figure 6, the "+ Enzyme inhibitor" bar rises to 240% of baseline, while the "+ Enzyme inducer" bar falls to 42%. For a patient on a stable dose of the substrate drug, which condition poses the greatest risk of toxicity?

options.A: Normal metabolism
options.B: Enzyme induction
options.C: Neither condition changes risk
options.D: Enzyme inhibition — because it raises the substrate drug’s blood level

quiz.why: The tallest bar in the chart is the enzyme-inhibitor condition at 240% of baseline — the substrate drug accumulates because it can no longer be cleared normally, raising toxicity risk. The inducer bar shows the opposite problem (42%, risking therapeutic failure), not toxicity.
quiz.label: Lecture check 1 · S8-9

quiz.stem: A patient stable on a CYP3A4-substrate medication with a narrow therapeutic index is started on a new drug that is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: No change, since CYP3A4 only affects Phase II metabolism
options.B: Decreased substrate drug level and reduced effect
options.C: Increased substrate drug level and increased toxicity risk
options.D: Increased renal clearance of the substrate drug

quiz.why: Inhibiting the CYP enzyme responsible for clearing the substrate drug slows its metabolism, raising its blood level — especially dangerous when the substrate has a narrow therapeutic index.
quiz.label: Lecture check 2 · S10-11

quiz.stem: A patient’s eGFR drops significantly due to new chronic kidney disease. For a drug that is primarily renally eliminated, what dosing adjustment is most appropriate?

options.A: No adjustment is needed
options.B: Increase the dose
options.C: Switch to IV administration only
options.D: Decrease the dose and/or extend the dosing interval

quiz.why: Reduced renal clearance raises drug exposure for renally-eliminated drugs; the standard response is a lower dose, a longer interval, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl.
quiz.label: Lecture check 3 · S16-17

quiz.stem: Using Figure 7, approximately what percentage of the original drug concentration remains after 3 half-lives (3 t½)?
quiz.why: Each half-life cuts the remaining concentration in half: 100% → 50% (1 t½) → 25% (2 t½) → 12.5% (3 t½), exactly as marked on the curve. By 5 half-lives the drug is roughly 97% eliminated (about 3% remaining).
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 4 · S21-22

quiz.stem: In Figure 8, the dashed orange line (loading dose + maintenance) starts at the target concentration immediately, while the solid teal line (maintenance only) climbs gradually over several doses. What is the clinical advantage of adding a loading dose?

options.A: It permanently lowers the maintenance dose needed
options.B: It eliminates the need for monitoring
options.C: It has no advantage over maintenance dosing alone
options.D: It reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives

quiz.why: The dashed loading-dose curve starts at the dotted steady-state line from the very first dose, while the solid maintenance-only curve needs several dosing intervals (~4–5 half-lives) to climb to that same level — exactly as defined on the previous slide. A loading dose does not change the maintenance dose itself or remove the need for monitoring.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 5 · S25-26

quiz.stem: Approximately how many half-lives are required for a drug to reach steady state with regular, repeated dosing?

options.D: Steady state is reached immediately after the first dose

quiz.why: Steady state — where drug intake equals drug elimination — is reached in roughly 4–5 half-lives, regardless of dose size. This is also why a drug is roughly 97% eliminated about 5 half-lives after stopping it.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 6 · S29-30

quiz.stem: A patient is found to carry the HLA-B*5801 allele before starting allopurinol. Why does this matter clinically?

options.A: It identifies a sharply increased risk of a severe hypersensitivity reaction
options.B: It predicts reduced drug absorption
options.C: It only affects how the drug tastes
options.D: It has no bearing on drug selection

quiz.why: HLA-B*5801 is associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol — a textbook pharmacogenomic screening consideration you will see again in Thursday’s gout lecture.
quiz.label: Lecture check 7 · S35-36

quiz.stem: Before prescribing any new medication, which single check is most directly aimed at preventing a toxic, often-predictable drug-drug interaction?

options.A: Confirming the drug’s brand name
options.B: Checking the drug’s chemical name
options.C: Reviewing the drug’s half-life alone
options.D: Reviewing CYP450 interactions with the patient’s current medications

quiz.why: CYP450 interaction screening is one of the single highest-yield steps for preventing predictable, preventable toxicity before adding any new drug to a regimen.
quiz.topic: Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making
quiz.label: Lecture check 8 · S42-43

quiz.stem: A drug has high potency but low efficacy compared to an alternative. For a patient needing maximum symptom relief, which factor matters more when choosing between the two?

options.A: Efficacy
options.B: Potency
options.C: Both matter equally
options.D: Neither predicts clinical benefit

quiz.why: Efficacy (the maximum achievable effect) matters more than potency for most clinical outcomes.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 9 · S46; S48

quiz.stem: A patient with CKD is prescribed a renally-cleared, narrow-TI drug without dose adjustment. Which two consequences would you expect together?

options.A: Decreased half-life and decreased concentration
options.B: Increased clearance and decreased Vd
options.C: Increased half-life and increased concentration
options.D: No change in either parameter

quiz.why: Reduced renal clearance raises both drug concentration and half-life.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 10 · S46; S48

quiz.stem: Which best differentiates a competitive antagonist from a noncompetitive antagonist?

options.A: Competitive lowers Emax; noncompetitive does not
options.B: Noncompetitive lowers Emax; competitive shifts the curve right without changing Emax
options.C: They are pharmacologically identical
options.D: Only competitive antagonists cause adverse effects

quiz.why: Noncompetitive/irreversible antagonists lower Emax; competitive antagonists shift the curve right without changing Emax.
quiz.topic: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
quiz.label: Lecture check 11 · S46; S48

quiz.stem: Drug A, a CYP enzyme inducer, is started in a patient taking Drug B, a substrate of that same CYP enzyme. What happens to Drug B’s level and effect?

options.A: Increases, raising toxicity risk
options.B: No change
options.C: Drug B’s route of elimination changes to biliary

quiz.stem: A 68-year-old woman with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min) is starting a narrow-TI oral antiarrhythmic eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney. Three weeks ago she began a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What is the best step before the prescription is filled?

quiz.stem: In Figure 1, corticosteroids are shown blocking the pathway at the "Membrane Phospholipids → Arachidonic Acid" step, while NSAIDs act one step later. What does this positioning explain?
