brief.part: L01 · Part 1 · The Language of Pharmacology
hy: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body (receptors & effect).
ADR = unintended, harmful, at **normal therapeutic doses**; toxicity = dose/exposure **exceeds the therapeutic range**.
Learn, prescribe, and counsel by **generic name** — brand names can hide a shared ingredient → double-dosing.
Pharmacology connects a drug's chemistry to its clinical effect.
traps: "Therapeutic effect" and "pharmacologic effect" are not synonyms — a drug can have pharmacologic effects that are not therapeutic (that is often exactly what an adverse effect is).
ADR vs. toxicity: an ADR happens at normal therapeutic doses; toxicity happens when dose or exposure exceeds the therapeutic range.
Generic names do NOT vary by manufacturer (one per drug); brand names DO vary — and change between countries.

hy: **Efficacy** = ideal trial conditions; **effectiveness** = everyday practice (adherence, comorbidities).
Phase I healthy volunteers → II few hundred patients → III hundreds–thousands (confirm) → IV postmarketing.
Rare adverse effects (1 in 10,000) are often first found in Phase IV.
Risk-benefit is always comparative — ask "compared to what?"
traps: Efficacy vs. effectiveness is a favorite exam distinction: efficacy is the trial result; effectiveness is what happens once real patients with real adherence patterns use the drug.
Phase III — not Phase I, II, or IV — is the large pre-approval trial that confirms efficacy and monitors safety at scale.
Phase III is what most people picture as "the" clinical trial, but regulatory decisions already begin shaping the drug long before that.

hy: Drug → target → signal transduction → response.
Five target classes: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters, nucleic acids.
Competitive antagonist = curve **shifts right, same Emax**; noncompetitive/irreversible = **lower Emax**.
Inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal; an antagonist only blocks.
Pharmacodynamics explains how drugs bind receptors to produce agonism or antagonism.
traps: Classic exam trap: a competitive antagonist shifts the dose-response curve **right** (same Emax, more drug needed); a noncompetitive/irreversible antagonist **lowers the Emax** instead.

A rightward shift with an unchanged plateau is the graphical signature of competitive antagonism — potency falls, but because the antagonism is surmountable, enough agonist can still reach the original Emax.
Inverse agonist ≠ antagonist: only the inverse agonist lowers baseline activity below normal, without any agonist present.
Study-guide distractor: "has no effect on receptor activity whatsoever" matches none of the agonist/antagonist types.

hy: **Potency** = dose needed (EC₅₀, lower = more potent); **efficacy** = Emax (ceiling).
Potency and efficacy are independent; efficacy matters more clinically.
**TI = TD₅₀ ÷ ED₅₀**; narrow TI → careful dosing + blood-level monitoring.
Narrow-TI drugs: **warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin**.
traps: A drug can be very potent (tiny dose) but have low efficacy — potency alone never tells you whether a drug "works better."
Same Emax + lower dose needed = MORE POTENT, EQUALLY efficacious — not "more efficacious."
EC₅₀ measures potency — not toxicity and not bioavailability.
A narrow-TI drug is not "safer because it needs a lower dose" — it has a smaller margin and needs closer monitoring.

brief.part: L01 · Part 5 · Pharmacokinetics: ADME — Absorption & Distribution
hy: **F** = fraction of dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged; IV = 100%.
First-pass: oral → GI → portal → liver → systemic; big examples nitroglycerin, propranolol, morphine.
Every route except oral bypasses first-pass (sublingual = direct to systemic veins).
Only **free (unbound)** drug is active; high **Vd** = drug mostly in tissue (e.g., digoxin).
BBB: small, lipophilic, non-ionized drugs cross; P-glycoprotein pumps some back out.
traps: IV = 100% bioavailable with no absorption phase; oral is less than 100%.
Taking an oral drug with food or on an empty stomach does not bypass first-pass metabolism — sublingual does.
A very high Vd does not mean a big anatomic space — it means the drug is mostly in tissue, not plasma.
Only free (unbound) drug is active and can cross membranes — protein-bound drug cannot.

brief.part: L02 · Part 1 · Drug Metabolism & CYP450 Interactions
hy: Phase I (CYP450): oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis. Phase II: conjugation → water-soluble.
**Inhibitor → substrate ↑ → toxicity**; **inducer → substrate ↓ → therapeutic failure**.
Narrow-TI substrate + CYP inhibitor = especially dangerous.
Metabolism can produce toxic metabolites (e.g., NAPQI).
traps: Inhibitor → substrate level UP (toxicity); inducer → substrate level DOWN (therapeutic failure). Don't swap them.
CYP3A4 is a Phase I (CYP450) enzyme — it does not "only affect Phase II metabolism."
Not every drug goes through Phase I first — some go straight to Phase II conjugation.

brief.part: L02 · Part 2 · Drug Excretion & Renal Dosing
hy: Kidney = dominant elimination route; filtration (free drug), secretion (transporters), reabsorption (lipophilic, un-ionized).
**↓ renal function → ↓ clearance → ↑ exposure** → lower dose and/or longer interval, guided by **eGFR/CrCl**.
Renally cleared narrow-TI drugs: many antibiotics, digoxin, lithium.
traps: Only FREE (unbound) drug is filtered at the glomerulus.
Reabsorption REDUCES net elimination — and only lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed.
Renal impairment → lower dose and/or longer interval — NOT "no adjustment," a higher dose, or "IV only."

brief.part: L02 · Part 3 · PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance
hy: **t½** = time for plasma concentration to fall 50%; set by **clearance + Vd**.
Each t½ halves what remains: 50 → 25 → 12.5 → 6.25 → ~3% (~97% eliminated at 5 t½).
**Steady state ≈ 4–5 t½**, regardless of dose; loading dose gets there immediately.
**Clearance** = plasma volume cleared per unit time; total = hepatic + renal.
CKD: clearance ↓ → t½ ↑ → concentration ↑ → adjust dose and/or interval.
traps: After 3 half-lives, 12.5% REMAINS (87.5% eliminated) — read whether the question asks remaining or eliminated.
Time to steady state depends on half-life — not on dose size, bioavailability, or route.
Half-life is not a fixed property — it changes with clearance and Vd (e.g., in renal impairment).
A loading dose does NOT permanently lower the maintenance dose or eliminate monitoring.

hy: Pharmacogenomics = genetic variation changing drug response (metabolism, transport, target, ADR risk).
**HLA-B*5801 + allopurinol** → severe hypersensitivity risk.
CYP2D6–codeine; CYP2C19–clopidogrel; TPMT–azathioprine.
Genotype is **one input among several**.
traps: HLA-B*5801 before allopurinol = severe hypersensitivity risk — not absorption, not taste, and not irrelevant to drug selection.
Genotype is one input — never the sole basis for therapy.

brief.part: L02 · Part 5 · Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making
hy: Memorize the checklist: indication, contraindications/allergies, renal/hepatic, interactions (CYP450), age/pregnancy, dose/route/monitoring.
**Always check CYP450 interactions before adding a new drug.**
These five ideas are the toolkit for every drug class for the rest of the course, starting with musculoskeletal pharmacology.
traps: The single check most aimed at preventing a toxic, predictable drug-drug interaction is reviewing CYP450 interactions — not brand name, chemical name, or half-life alone.
Weaker home-medication effect + restored by a higher dose = competitive; not restored = irreversible.
Reviewing indication, contraindications, renal/hepatic function, interactions, and monitoring = the clinical decision-making framework — not pharmacogenomic testing or Phase IV surveillance.

brief.part: L03 · Part 1 · Musculoskeletal Pain & the Inflammatory Cascade
hy: Injury → mediators → nociceptor sensitization → pain.
Musculoskeletal pain is driven by inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, cytokines) — NSAIDs and corticosteroids intervene at different points along this cascade.
Corticosteroids = phospholipase A₂ (broad); NSAIDs = COX (prostaglandins).
Prostaglandins drive inflammatory pain, and COX makes them.
traps: Corticosteroids act **upstream** at phospholipase A₂, not at COX — that is why their effect is broader than an NSAID’s.
The lecture’s drugs target nociceptive and inflammatory pain; neuropathic pain is a different unit.

hy: Acetaminophen treats pain and fever but is not a reliable anti-inflammatory agent; its overdose toxicity is mediated by NAPQI accumulation.
Overdose: glutathione depleted → NAPQI → hepatocyte injury.
Antidote: N-acetylcysteine (glutathione precursor).
Ask about ALL sources — combination cold/flu/sleep products hide acetaminophen.
Acetaminophen is central, with no real anti-inflammatory effect. Overdose means NAPQI, and the antidote is NAC.

brief.part: L03 · Part 3 · NSAIDs & COX-2 Selective Inhibition
hy: COX-1 = housekeeping (gastric protection, renal blood flow); COX-2 = inflammation.
NSAIDs are effective but carry real GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk; celecoxib trades GI risk for cardiovascular risk (renal risk similar).
NSAID harms: GI, renal, cardiovascular.
Triple whammy: NSAID + ACEi/ARB + diuretic → AKI.
Ketorolac: short-term only; significant GI/renal risk.
COX-1 protects the stomach, platelets and kidney. Nonselective NSAIDs block both isoforms.
Celecoxib cuts GI risk but raises cardiovascular risk, and does not spare the kidney.

brief.part: L03 · Part 4 · Osteoarthritis, Rheumatoid Arthritis & DMARDs
hy: OA = degenerative → pain control; RA = autoimmune → suppress disease activity.
OA ladder: acetaminophen → oral or topical NSAIDs → intra-articular steroids for a single-joint flare.
DMARDs (conventional and biologic — methotrexate, adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, tocilizumab, rituximab, abatacept) modify RA’s disease course rather than only masking symptoms.
Methotrexate: DHFR inhibitor, **weekly**, with folate.
Methotrexate toxicity: liver, marrow, lung; teratogenic.
HCQ = milder RA; sulfasalazine = combinations; leflunomide = if MTX not tolerated.
DMARDs change disease. Methotrexate is weekly, and screen for TB and hepatitis before biologics.
TNF: adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab · IL-6: tocilizumab · B cell: rituximab · T-cell costimulation: abatacept.
Shared risk: immunosuppression → infection.
Before biologics: TB + hepatitis B/C screening, update (live) vaccines.

summary.text: Pharmacology studies how drugs interact with living systems: **pharmacokinetics** is what the body does to the drug (ADME), and **pharmacodynamics** is what the drug does to the body.
Learn and prescribe by **generic name** — brand names can hide a shared ingredient and cause unintentional double-dosing.
Drugs move from discovery through preclinical testing, **Phase I–III** trials, FDA review, and **Phase IV** postmarketing surveillance — where rare adverse effects are often first found.

Metabolism inactivates drugs, activates prodrugs, or makes active or **toxic metabolites** (e.g., NAPQI); **Phase I** (CYP450 oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) functionalizes and **Phase II** conjugates for excretion.
A **CYP inhibitor raises** a substrate's level (toxicity) and an **inducer lowers** it (therapeutic failure) — always check CYP450 interactions before adding a drug.
The **kidney** is the main elimination route — filtration of free drug, active secretion, reabsorption of lipophilic un-ionized drug — and less renal function means less clearance and more exposure.
Tissue injury releases **prostaglandins, bradykinin, histamine, and cytokines** that sensitize nociceptors; **corticosteroids** block phospholipase A₂ upstream, while **NSAIDs** block COX.
